opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one of the things I find most interesting about where the field is right now. For a long time, the way we evaluated image generation was through proxy metrics, things like FID or CLIP score, and those were useful for tracking progress early on, but they really don't capture what people actually care about when they look at an image. You can have a model that scores well on FID and still produces images that people find kind of bland or off in subtle ways.

So the way I think about it is in a few stages. First, you have pretraining, where the model learns this enormous distribution of what images look like and how they relate to text. That gives you breadth and capability, but the pretraining distribution is the internet, and the internet is full of mediocre images. If you just sample from that distribution faithfully, you get something that's, on average, average.

Then the question becomes, how do you shift the model toward the part of that distribution that people actually prefer? Part of that is data curation and fine-tuning on high-aesthetic, high-quality subsets. That alone gets you surprisingly far. But to really go further, you want a signal that reflects human judgment directly, and that's where preference data comes in. You show people pairs of images for the same prompt and ask which one they prefer, or rate them along different axes like prompt adherence, aesthetics, and artifacts, and you use that either to train a reward model or to directly optimize the generator with something like a DPO-style objective adapted for diffusion.

The tricky part at large scale is that "human preference" isn't one thing. People disagree, and they disagree in structured ways. Some people want photorealism, some want a strong stylized look, some care most about the model doing exactly what the prompt said. If you collapse all of that into a single scalar reward and optimize hard against it, you tend to get mode collapse toward a particular look. Everything starts to have the same glossy, high-contrast, over-saturated aesthetic. It wins head-to-head comparisons, but you lose diversity and you lose the ability to serve people whose taste differs from the median.

So a lot of the work is in being careful about that. Separating out the different dimensions of preference so you're not trading off prompt faithfulness for prettiness without realizing it. Regularizing so the model doesn't drift too far from its base distribution. And thinking about personalization or controllability, so instead of finding the single image everyone likes, you give people the levers to get what they like.

The other thing I'd say is that reward hacking is very real in images. Reward models have blind spots, and a generator optimized against them will find those blind spots. So you need ongoing human evaluation as a check, not just the automated reward, and you need to refresh your preference data as the model gets better, because what people preferred a year ago against a weaker model isn't necessarily informative about the frontier today.

Ultimately, I think the goal isn't to maximize a number. It's to build models that are genuinely useful creative tools, and human preference is our best handle on that, as long as we remember it's a pretty noisy and pluralistic handle.

r001.rationale: The response says hard optimization can cause mode collapse into the same glossy, high-contrast, over-saturated look, losing diversity and distinctiveness.

r002.rationale: It recommends personalization and controllability so users can steer the model toward the styles and preferences they like.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because when you're working on a model that's going to be used by many millions of people, the question of "what is a good image" stops being an aesthetic question and becomes a statistical one. And it's a really hard one, because preferences are not monolithic.

The way I tend to frame it is that there are a few layers. The first layer is just correctness: does the image actually depict what the prompt asked for? Did you get the right number of objects, the right spatial relationships, is the text rendered correctly, are the hands okay. That layer is almost universal. Nobody wants a sixth finger. So you can push pretty hard on that with fairly standard techniques, whether that's better captioning on the training side, or preference data and some form of reinforcement learning or direct preference optimization on the post-training side, and you're not really trading off against anyone.

The second layer is aesthetics, and that's where it gets interesting, because now you're averaging over people who genuinely disagree. If you collect a large pool of pairwise comparisons and train a reward model on them, you get something that encodes the median taste of your rater pool. And the median taste tends to like high contrast, saturated colors, dramatic lighting, centered subjects, bokeh. If you then optimize against that reward model hard enough, you converge on a very particular "AI look" that everybody can now recognize. So one of the things I think a lot about is how not to collapse diversity. You want the model to be able to produce a flat, muted, documentary-style photo when that's what the prompt implies, and not have it dragged toward the glossy mean.

There are a few ways to address that. One is to be careful about what you ask raters. "Which image do you prefer" is a very different question from "which image better matches this prompt" or "which image looks more like a real photograph." You can decompose preference into components and then decide how to weight them, rather than letting a single scalar absorb everything. Another is to condition on the user or on the style, so that the model learns that preferences are contextual rather than global. And another is just regularization: you don't want to move too far from your base distribution, because the base distribution has a lot of real-world variety in it that the preference signal will happily erase.

The third layer, which I think is underappreciated, is that the reward model itself is a model, and it will be exploited. Any time you optimize against a learned proxy, you'll find the places where the proxy is wrong. We've seen this with text, where models learn to be verbose because raters like length, and the same thing happens with images. The reward model likes a certain kind of texture, so the generator adds that texture everywhere. So you need a loop where you keep collecting fresh human data on the current model's outputs, retrain the reward model, and keep it honest. It's never a one-shot thing.

And then finally, I'd say the measurement matters as much as the optimization. You can look at win rates in a controlled study, but what you really care about is whether people actually use the images, whether they regenerate, whether they edit, whether they come back. Those behavioral signals are noisy but they're closer to the truth than a lab rating. So I try to think of preference optimization as a combination of explicit comparisons, which are clean but narrow, and implicit signals, which are messy but reflect what people really want. Getting those to agree is kind of the whole game.

r001.rationale: The response says optimizing for median taste can produce a recognizable “AI look” and drag varied styles toward a glossy mean, conveying generic output with less distinctive character.

r002.rationale: It identifies conditioning on the user or style so preferences are contextual rather than global, which communicates tailoring image generation to individual stylistic preferences.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is: what do we mean by human preference? With image generation, there are several things people care about. Does the image look good? Does it actually follow the prompt? And does it match the style or intent that the person had in mind? Those things overlap, but they’re not identical. You can generate a beautiful image that completely misses what someone asked for.

One way to approach this is to collect comparisons: given a prompt and two generated images, which one does a person prefer? You can use those judgments to train a preference model, and then use that model to guide the generator’s training. That gives you a more scalable signal than asking a human to evaluate every training step.

But the challenge is that the preference model is still a proxy. If you optimize against it too aggressively, you can get better at satisfying that model without actually making images that people like more. So I’d want fresh human evaluations throughout, including on prompts and use cases that weren’t represented in the training data.

And I wouldn’t think of human preference as a single universal ranking. People have different tastes. The goal should be to improve the things that are broadly useful, like following instructions, while preserving diversity and giving the individual user control over the result.

r001.rationale: The response warns that optimizing a proxy can diverge from human preferences, but does not say this can produce generic images lacking distinctive character.

r002.rationale: It mentions preserving diversity and giving users control, but does not identify control tailored to each user’s stylistic preferences as an approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is, what do we actually mean by human preference? For image generation, people might care about visual quality, whether the image follows the prompt, or whether it captures a particular style. Those things don’t always move together, and different people will weigh them differently.

One practical approach is to collect comparisons: given a prompt and two generated images, which one does someone prefer? You can use those judgments to train a preference model, and then use that model to guide the generator. But the challenge is making sure you’re improving what people actually want, rather than just getting better at exploiting the preference model.

So I’d think of it as an iterative process. Collect diverse feedback, optimize against it, and then evaluate with fresh human judgments. And I’d want to look beyond a single average score. Are we improving prompt adherence? Are we preserving diversity? Are there groups of users whose preferences we’re consistently missing? At scale, those questions become just as important as the optimization algorithm.

r001.rationale: The response discusses visual quality, prompt adherence, and style as distinct preferences, but does not say optimization may yield generic images lacking distinctive character.

r002.rationale: It notes that people weigh preferences differently and asks whether groups are being missed, but does not identify user-specific stylistic control as an approach.
